title: Victim's lawyers back closed testimony, stronger protection for Duterte ICC trial witnesses
summary: PRAGUE, Czech Republic - Amid the “exceptional circumstances” in former President Rodrigo Duterte"s International Criminal Court (ICC) case, closed sessions and stronger protections for testifying…
byline: Andy Peñafuerte III, Jay-vee Marasigan Pangan

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 1:56am

PRAGUE, Czech Republic – Amid the “exceptional circumstances” in former President Rodrigo Duterte’s International Criminal Court (ICC) case, closed sessions and stronger protections for testifying witnesses are necessary, the victims’ lawyers tell the Trial Chamber III.

While Common Legal Representatives of the Victims (CLRV) Gilbert Andres, Joel Butuyan, and Paolina Massidda back the Office of the Prosecutor’s request for in-court protective measures for victims and witnesses, they suggest the court adopt a “comprehensive and prospective approach” in its assessment.

In particular, the lawyers request the use of closed sessions “for all the testimony” of most witnesses, combined with pseudonyms and voice distortions for “effective protection,” given the “objectively justifiable risks” these individuals face.

“The pseudonym would prevent the formal identification of the witness in the proceedings, while closed session testimony would prevent the disclosure of the substantive and contextual details capable of revealing [REDACTED] identity,” the lawyers argued in their filing released on November 19.
Political and social context

The prosecution had earlier sought protective and special measures for 55 witnesses expected to testify in Duterte’s trial, including pseudonyms, face and voice distortion, private or closed sessions, and psychological support for some witnesses.

The victims’ lawyers said public hearings remain a fundamental principle at the ICC, but that openness must be balanced against the Court’s obligation to protect the safety, physical and psychological well-being, dignity and privacy of victims and witnesses.

Noting the “particular political and social context” of Duterte’s case, the CLRVs said conventional protective measures “do not necessarily eliminate the risk of identification,” particularly when details disclosed during testimony could reveal a witness’s identity.

The CLRVs also urged judges to consider risks to witnesses’ families, saying that in the Philippines’ “close-knit communities and family-oriented social context”, the consequences of identifying a witness could extend beyond the person testifying.

In another redacted section, the lawyers said public identification in the “prevailing political and social climate in the Philippines” could expose a witness to a “real risk of harm, intimidation and/or social ostracism.”
“Accordingly, in adjudicating the Request, the Chamber should consider not only the risks faced by the witness, but also the foreseeable repercussions [REDACTED] family.”
Participating victims and witnesses
The ICC’s page on Duterte’s case states that Trial Chamber III has authorized more than 500 victims to participate in the proceedings set to open on November 30.
“More victims may apply and be authorised to participate in the trial,” the page stated.
Victims and witnesses have different roles in ICC proceedings.

“Witnesses give evidence in Court to help establish the facts of a case. They may be eyewitnesses, people with inside knowledge, or experts. Victims could also be witnesses or be authorized by the judges to appear and present their own views before the Court.

Participating victims have suffered harm from crimes related to the case and have been granted the right to participate by the judges. Participating victims are represented by their own representative/lawyer in the courtroom, who represents their views and concerns.”

The ICC said its obligation to protect the safety, physical and psychological well-being, dignity and privacy of victims and witnesses starts from the investigation and continues throughout the proceedings.
“Intimidating or interfering with witnesses at any stage of the investigations or the proceedings can constitute an offence against the administration of justice at the ICC.”
The ICC also reminds the public that the identities of protected witnesses remain confidential and must be respected.
“Respecting witnesses means respecting the justice process.” — BAP, GMA News
